title: Evaporative Emissions: How Fuel Vapor Is Managed
introduction: Fuel can leave the tank as vapor as well as liquid. I think of EVAP as a holding room with a useful exit: it captures vapor, then sends it to the engine to be burned rather than letting it escape into the air. This overview identifies the components in the EcoBoost application named on this page and separates their basic jobs. It is a system guide, not a leak test or replacement procedure.

edits.text: The EVAP system keeps hydrocarbon emissions out of the atmosphere by storing fuel vapors, then routing those vapors to the engine for consumption during normal engine operation.
edits.why: Storage and later consumption are the central idea: the system manages fuel vapor rather than simply releasing it outside.

edits.text: Use these component names to distinguish the storage, flow-control, pressure-sensing and filler parts of the EVAP system:
edits.why: I keep the names separate because a canister, a valve and a sensor describe different jobs, even when they belong to the same vapor system.

edits.text: EVAP canister — captures and stores fuel vapor in activated carbon until that vapor is drawn toward the engine during purging.
edits.why: Purging makes the carbon available to capture more vapor. The canister is the storage component, distinct from the valves controlling its routes.

edits.text: EVAP canister purge valve — electrically regulates the flow of stored fuel vapor from the canister toward the engine intake.
edits.why: “Purge” identifies the engine-bound route; it helps distinguish this valve from the outside-air control.

edits.text: EVAP canister vent solenoid — electrically controls the canister’s connection to outside air.
edits.why: The vent route and the purge route serve different purposes. Similar valve names do not make the components interchangeable.

edits.text: EVAP blocking valve — a distinct system component to identify separately from the purge valve and vent solenoid.
edits.why: This overview identifies the blocking valve without describing its operating sequence or service connections.

edits.text: Fuel Tank Pressure (FTP) sensor and tube — the tank-pressure sensing components included in this system.
edits.why: This name identifies a sensing function rather than vapor storage or flow control; it does not supply a pressure test or an acceptable reading.

edits.text: Easy Fuel (capless) fuel tank filler pipe — the capless filler component included in the EVAP system.
edits.why: Keep the filler pipe in the system picture alongside the canister, valves and pressure-sensing components.
